channel_name: Invest Like the Best · Patrick O'Shaughnessy
video_title: The AI Selloff Doesn't Match the Data | Top AI Investor Explains
gist: An AI-focused investor (Gavin), fresh off a week of meetings in Silicon Valley, argues the July 2026 AI stock selloff (AI names down 40-60%) is disconnected from fundamentals: GPU rental prices, DRAM spot prices, and token growth are all accelerating, not decelerating, and Nvidia trades at its lowest forward P/E in a decade. The core bull thesis rests on the spread between legacy long-term GPU contracts and a much higher current spot market repricing hyperscaler operating cash flow upward, reducing the AI buildout's need for debt financing; the biggest risks he identifies are regulatory backlash and (more speculatively) a breakthrough in continual/sample-efficient learning.

themes.theme: The AI Selloff Doesn't Match On-the-Ground Fundamentals

insights.claim: Despite AI-related stocks falling roughly 40-60% from their highs in a straight line during July 2026, the investor could not find a single quantitative metric showing AI deceleration after actively searching for one all week in Silicon Valley; GPU availability, GPU rental pricing, DRAM spot prices, and token growth were all accelerating.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: A disconnect this wide between price action and fundamentals is a classic setup investors should watch for mean reversion or further confirmation of deceleration before following the tape down.
insights.quote: Loads of AI names are down 50 60% from their highs. We'll call it 40 to 60% in a month in a straight line.

insights.claim: Nvidia's forward P/E is at its lowest level in the last ten years as of early August 2026, a valuation level previously only seen during the 'Liberation Day' tariff scare and the DeepSeek panic, both of which turned out to be V-shaped bottoms.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Historical precedent (Liberation Day, DeepSeek) suggests these valuation troughs have previously marked buying opportunities rather than the start of a structural derating.
insights.quote: Nvidia is actually, as we record this, at its lowest forward PE of the last 10 years.

insights.claim: The guest describes himself as more bearish than nearly everyone he met during a week of meetings across the AI ecosystem in Silicon Valley, despite actively trying to pressure-test and find reasons to be scared about AI valuations.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: When even a skeptic doing a dedicated bear-case search comes back more bullish than industry insiders, it signals the marginal information available to public-market investors is unusually one-sided toward optimism.
insights.quote: essentially everyone out here is more bullish than me, man.

insights.claim: The only negative data point the guest could find after actively searching was third-party data suggesting Anthropic's growth curve deviated slightly off trajectory -- a claim he notes is hotly contested by Anthropic shareholders who have an incentive (an eventual IPO allocation) to argue the company is doing well, and which is more than offset by accelerating growth at OpenAI and in open-source models.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Anthropic's growth trajectory is the one genuine soft spot in an otherwise accelerating AI data picture and is worth monitoring independently, given the incentive conflicts around who reports on it.
insights.quote: the main thing people are saying is the anthropic like the third party data suggests that the anthropic like curve started to go off of its trajectory a little bit. That's like the only thing

insights.claim: Unlike prior scares (2022 rates/recession fears, the DeepSeek shock, Liberation Day tariffs) where the market knew exactly what it was pricing, the July 2026 AI selloff is unusual because the specific narratives cited (Meta capex cuts, open-source disruption, DUV lithography news) all turned out to be factually wrong except for the credit/spread widening, making the ongoing decline harder to explain and, to a technician, more worrying precisely because there's no obvious catalyst left to blame.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: A selloff without an identifiable fundamental cause is technically more dangerous than one with a clear narrative, since it may reflect positioning/flows rather than information investors can act on.
insights.quote: You know, it's definitionally the bullet you don't see that gets you.

insights.claim: A friend at Fidelity described the most effective strategy over the last three years as mechanically cutting risk in response to any scary-sounding AI headline and cycling between narratives, rather than doing fundamental analysis.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: If reflexive, headline-driven de-risking has been the dominant winning behavior, it implies current selling may be more mechanical/momentum-driven than fundamentally justified.
insights.quote: the way to have navigated like the last three years is just do the dumbest most superficial thing as quickly as possible and just cycle between them.

insights.claim: A large share of public-market investors now feed every incoming AI-related headline through Claude for interpretation before trading on it, which the guest argues collapses the normal diversity of investor opinion that cushions markets against overreaction, echoing a theory (attributed to a strategist referred to as 'Mikeson') that a breakdown in diversity of views precedes bubbles and crashes.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: If a large fraction of trading flow is effectively taking direction from one AI model's interpretation of news, market reactions to ambiguous headlines may be larger and more correlated than fundamentals justify -- a structural fragility worth pricing in.
insights.quote: Claude is kind of Walter Kronite for the stock market

insights.claim: An anonymous semiconductor analyst posted that Japanese capacitor stocks had compressed what would normally be a multi-year cycle into six weeks, with share prices doubling, tripling, or quadrupling before the underlying earnings fundamentals had even caught up.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Compressed, reflexive multi-year cycles happening in weeks is a sign of speculative excess in specific AI supply-chain pockets that could reverse sharply even if the broader AI infrastructure thesis holds.
insights.quote: We've had a capacitor an entire capacitor cycle in 6 weeks.

themes.theme: The Spot-vs-Contract GPU Price Gap Is the Key Bull Signal

insights.claim: A cluster of several thousand Blackwell B200 GPUs currently renting at roughly $2 per GPU-hour is contracted to rise to just under $4 per GPU-hour seven months from now for the exact same hardware -- a 50-60% price increase over a period when many bears expected prices to decline.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Rising, not falling, GPU rental rates on identical hardware is the single clearest real-time signal that AI compute demand is outstripping supply, contradicting the bear thesis of imminent price collapse.
insights.quote: They're renting the exact same cluster, exact same size cluster, essentially identical in every way, B200s, no no differences, and they're hoping seven months later to pay just under $4.

insights.claim: An inference-cloud provider stated publicly that it expects to pay 100% more for Blackwell GPUs once its current long-term contract expires, implying hyperscalers who locked in older, lower-priced contracts are systematically under-earning relative to the current spot market.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: As legacy contracts roll off across the industry, this dynamic implies a structural, multi-quarter tailwind to hyperscaler compute revenue and operating cash flow independent of new capex.
insights.quote: we are planning to pay 100% more for blackwells when our contract expires

insights.claim: Because most installed AI compute is still priced off legacy 2024-2025 long-term offtake contracts signed far below today's spot market, hyperscaler operating cash flow should keep accelerating as those contracts roll off and reprice to current (higher) spot levels, even if spot prices themselves later plateau or ease somewhat.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: This spread between contracted and spot pricing is a forward-looking, quantifiable driver of hyperscaler cash flow that investors can track directly instead of relying on capex headlines alone.

insights.claim: No one in 2024 or 2025 -- bull or bear -- modeled a scenario where prices for older-generation GPUs would still be rising in 2026; bulls expected a slow decline and bears expected a steep one, and reality has diverged from both assumptions.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: When actual outcomes fall outside the full range investors modeled a year or two earlier, it's a strong signal that consensus models (and current bear positioning) may still be miscalibrated.
insights.quote: I don't think anyone in 24 or 25 thought that the prices of old GPUs would still be would be going vertical in 2026.

insights.claim: Meta's plan to rent out excess compute capacity was interpreted by the market as bearish evidence of overcapacity and led to speculation of capex cuts, but the guest argues the opposite is true: Meta sold trading-optimized clusters at a large premium to its own contracted rates, demonstrating pricing power, and internal telemetry into Meta's capex plans showed no reduction -- if anything, plans grew more aggressive.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: A move the market priced as a negative catalyst was actually evidence of compute scarcity and pricing power, illustrating how misread single data points can drive outsized selloffs in AI infrastructure names.
insights.quote: None of that telemetry had shifted at all.

insights.claim: Shortly after the market misread Meta's compute-rental news as bearish, Meta released its best AI model in a long time (Muse 1.1), which the guest calls a genuinely strong model overshadowed by Grok 4.5's release -- further evidence Meta is not pulling back on AI investment.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Model-quality progress alongside compute-rental news confirms Meta's AI investment is accelerating, not retrenching, reinforcing the bull case on hyperscaler capex durability.

themes.theme: Hyperscaler Cash Flow and the Credit-Financing Question

insights.claim: Consensus models assume upcoming Blackwell and Rubin GPU generations will monetize at roughly the rate of the two-generations-old Ampere chip, which the guest views as an unrealistically bearish assumption given real-world demand signals from private AI companies.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: If consensus monetization assumptions are too conservative, current Street models understate future hyperscaler operating cash flow, implying upside to AI infrastructure earnings estimates.

insights.claim: Hyperscalers are estimated to be sitting on roughly $1.3-1.4 trillion of operating cash flow; if the installed compute base reprices even at a discount to current Blackwell spot rates (rather than at the more conservative Ampere-era rate assumed by consensus), that operating cash flow rises to roughly $2 trillion, removing about $700 billion of the credit/debt financing the market fears will be needed to fund the AI buildout.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: This is a concrete, testable framework for whether the AI buildout needs debt financing -- watch reported hyperscaler operating cash flow growth as the key variable determining credit-market risk to the AI trade.
insights.quote: then it's more like two trillion of operating cash flow and that kind of takes 700 billion of credit demand out

insights.claim: Reported operating cash flow from Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon accelerated quarter-over-quarter from roughly 28% growth to about 32% growth, and to roughly 35% after adjusting for an unusually large amount of one-time items (mostly EU-related legal expenses) -- a material acceleration at this scale, before Rubin chips come online or older contracts reprice.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Accelerating hyperscaler operating cash flow growth, ahead of further tailwinds from contract repricing and next-gen chips, directly undercuts the narrative that the AI buildout is running out of internal funding capacity.

insights.claim: July 2026 saw real warning signs in credit markets -- real yields rose, credit spreads widened, CDS blew out across AI-adjacent names, and a Meta bond priced worse than expected -- but the guest attributes much of this to banks hedging their financing commitments rather than genuine credit stress, noting the overwhelming majority of the AI buildout is still funded from operating cash flow, not debt.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Distinguishing technical credit-market hedging flows from genuine credit deterioration is critical for investors trying to judge whether widening AI-related spreads are a leading indicator of real financing stress.
insights.quote: These are just banks, you know, kind of hedging hedging their commitments.

insights.claim: The classic 'capital cycle' risk -- an AI buildout financed increasingly with debt that demands immediate repayment if supply and demand fall out of balance, as happened during the dot-com-era telecom buildout -- is the scenario the guest most wanted to stress-test this trip, and he concludes actual credit dependency is smaller than feared given the reacceleration in operating cash flow.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: The debt-fueled-overbuild scenario remains the single biggest structural risk to the AI trade and is the one to keep monitoring even if current data argues it's less imminent than the market priced in July.
insights.quote: debt fueled buildouts you know they demand immediate repayment. So if supply and demand get a little bit out of whack, things can unwind very very quickly. That's what happened in the internet

insights.claim: Even if credit does become scarce or expensive for financing future GPU buildouts, that outcome is not necessarily bearish for owners of existing compute -- it would simply mean the flops that do get built become scarcer and more valuable.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Investors worried about a credit crunch in AI infrastructure should distinguish between bearish for new capex growth versus bullish for the pricing power of already-installed compute.
insights.quote: if credit's not there, it just means the flops that are there are going to be even more valuable.

themes.theme: Open Source Models Expand the Compute Pie Rather Than Shrink It

insights.claim: The market treated the rise of open-source models (GLM 5.2, Kimi K3) as bearish for AI infrastructure spending, but the guest argues a token costs the same amount of compute, memory, and power to produce regardless of which model generates it -- so open-source share gains mostly reallocate margin dollars away from frontier labs' very high gross margins toward the infrastructure layer, while price elasticity increases total token demand.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Open-source model progress should be read as compute-demand-neutral-to-positive rather than negative for AI infrastructure spending, reframing a key bear narrative from July 2026.
insights.quote: a token is a token, and you need the exact same amount of compute to make a token. and all else equal. It takes the same amount of flops, the same amount of memory, the same amount of watts.

insights.claim: A widely watched token-volume index (the 'Silicon Data' token index) dipped and flattened around the release of GLM 5.2 and Kimi K3 not because total token volume fell, but because the index's tracked mix shifted toward cheaper open-source tokens and away from higher-margin frontier tokens, creating a false appearance of deceleration.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Investors relying on public token-volume indices should understand their mix-shift blind spots before concluding AI usage growth is slowing.

insights.claim: When companies deploy a router that sends queries to the cheapest adequate model (often a fine-tuned open-source model, escalating to a frontier model only when needed), it can reduce reported AI spend while leaving GPU-hours consumed flat or even increasing them, because the savings come from lower margin per token, not from using less compute.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: A company's reported AI budget cuts don't necessarily translate into lower underlying compute demand -- investors should separate spend trends from GPU-hour trends when assessing infrastructure demand.

insights.claim: The guest expects the AI industry's future to be 'multimodel,' with AI-native companies increasingly fine-tuning open-source models with proprietary data and routing between them and frontier models to get similar or better outcomes at roughly half the cost, while remaining more defensible than a pure 'wrapper' around one frontier API.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: The multimodel trend favors infrastructure and tooling layers (routers, fine-tuning platforms) over any single frontier lab capturing all economic value from AI applications.
insights.quote: I do really think the future is like multi multimodel.

insights.claim: Fireworks AI's 'Nexus' product lets any AI-native company using tools like Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, or Grok ingest its own usage data with roughly 20 words of code, reinforcement-learning-tune an open-source model, and route queries between that model and frontier models -- a productized path from being a 'ChatGPT wrapper' to a defensible product, cited as a reason Cursor and Harvey leaned heavily into this approach.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Inference-cloud platforms that make model customization trivially easy are becoming a key moat-building layer for AI-native software companies, worth tracking as a distinct investable category.
insights.quote: if you're using cloud code, openAI codeex, grock build, it is literally three lines of code like 20 words and um fireworks ingests your data

insights.claim: A bear case exists in which, once a frontier model achieves recursive self-improvement, it could serve every level of intelligence at dramatically lower cost via distillation, eliminating any role for open-source models -- the guest calls this the 'Anthropic/OpenAI/Grok maximalist view' and considers it possible but unlikely, partly because AI-native companies have already built proprietary domain-specific data moats that give them independence from any single frontier provider.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: This is the key scenario that would most threaten the open-source/inference-cloud investment thesis, and is worth monitoring via frontier labs' cost-to-serve trends.

insights.claim: Inference-cloud businesses such as Fireworks, Base10, Modal, and Together are reportedly growing almost as fast as frontier labs did in their early days while burning comparatively little cash, an unusually capital-efficient growth profile for the category.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: These private inference-cloud companies represent a fast-growing, capital-efficient part of the AI stack that public-market investors largely can't see or price directly, a gap the guest flags as distorting the public narrative.

themes.theme: Nvidia's Financing Innovation and Competitive Moat

insights.claim: Nvidia has built what the guest calls a 'credit wrapper' business model -- taking equity stakes in AI companies plus a revenue share once GPU rental prices clear a floor -- effectively creating a large royalty-based, cloud-like revenue stream without directly lending money to GPU buyers (someone else provides the underlying financing).
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: This financing structure could scale into a very large, high-margin recurring revenue stream for Nvidia that is not well captured in standard chip-revenue-based valuation models, and should be modeled explicitly.
insights.quote: which I would describe as kind of like a credit wrapper um with a revenue share if GPU prices are above a floor

insights.claim: Nvidia writes clauses into its equity investments prohibiting the invested capital from being used to buy Nvidia chips, but since money is fungible, the guest notes this restriction is largely symbolic.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Nvidia's equity-investment ecosystem effectively recycles capital back toward its own chip sales regardless of contractual language, a dynamic investors should factor into assessments of demand durability.
insights.quote: Nvidia said that they write into all their you know equity investments that um you know the money can't be used to buy Nvidia chips but obviously money is fungeible

insights.claim: The guest argues nearly every time Nvidia has NOT taken an equity stake in a major AI company it has turned out to be a mistake -- citing Nvidia's initial absence from Anthropic's cap table before it later took a stake -- and that Nvidia's combination of equity upside plus recurring revenue share both bridges the AI industry's free-cash-flow gap and strengthens Nvidia's competitive position relative to AMD, Google's TPUs, and Amazon's Trainium chips, whose customers face harder financing terms and higher input costs.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Nvidia's financing ecosystem is becoming a structural moat, not just a chip-performance moat, that could sustain its market share even as competing chip architectures improve technically.
insights.quote: essentially every time they haven't taken an equity stake in something, it's been a mistake.

insights.claim: Given Nvidia's financing advantages, its role matchmaking land, power, and chip supply for buyers, and its new royalty-style revenue model, the guest finds it hard to understand why Nvidia trades at such a low valuation multiple.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: This is a direct valuation call: the guest sees Nvidia's current multiple as mispriced relative to its financing-driven competitive advantages, independent of its chip roadmap.
insights.quote: nothing's more financable than an Nvidia GPU nothing

themes.theme: Memory, Long-Term Agreements, and the Chip 'Game of Thrones'

insights.claim: Only four suppliers matter at scale for AI compute and memory -- Amazon (Trainium), Google (TPUs), AMD, and Nvidia (far larger than the other three combined) -- and long-term supply agreements (LTAs) with memory makers, in which customers prepay with a price floor and ceiling, have become the central axis around which competitive positioning in AI infrastructure now revolves.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Understanding LTA structures and who holds allocation priority is now more important to forecasting AI infrastructure winners than tracking spot chip prices alone.

insights.claim: Because future GPU and memory market share is increasingly determined by pre-purchased supply-chain allocation rather than spot buying, breaking a long-term agreement (LTA) to chase a lower price is now existentially risky: if supply later tightens again (a near-certainty in a cyclical industry where oversupply is followed by undersupply), the supplier deprioritizes the buyer who broke its agreement in favor of loyal customers, which could put that buyer out of business.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: This game-theoretic dynamic implies LTA-committed demand is unusually 'sticky' and unlikely to be broken even during a temporary price downturn, supporting the durability of current supply-chain commitments.
insights.quote: If you break your LTA and then in the next two or three years for any reason leverage shifts back to the memory guys you're out of business.

insights.claim: Adding more memory (HBM DRAM) per unit of compute is 'the single most important' lever for increasing tokens produced per unit of compute, which is why memory demand has shown no negative price elasticity despite rising memory costs -- it's the dominant axis affecting output, overriding other cost considerations.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Memory suppliers with the ability to expand HBM DRAM capacity have outsized pricing power and strategic leverage in AI infrastructure buildouts, a dynamic that should factor into memory-sector investment theses.
insights.quote: the more memory you put with flop for a given unit of compute, the more tokens you get out. It's the single most important thing you could do to increase kind of token output per unit of compute

insights.claim: The guest predicts other chip/memory suppliers (referencing SK Hynix specifically, spelled 'Highix' in the transcript) will try to replicate Nvidia's 'credit wrapper' financing model by putting up capital to backstop GPU/memory buyers' debt in exchange for a revenue-share cut, describing it as a logical extension of the LTA structure, and notes private credit firms are likely already pitching similar structures to memory companies.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Watch for memory and alternative-chip suppliers announcing Nvidia-style revenue-share financing deals as a signal that this structure is becoming an industry standard rather than an Nvidia-specific advantage.
insights.quote: I would be going to the buyers of GPUs, tradeiums, and whoever, and saying I'll participate in the Nvidia credit wrapper.

themes.theme: China's DUV Breakthrough and the Compute Decoupling

insights.claim: News that China obtained a DUV lithography capability (with some unconfirmed reports of a smuggled EUV machine) is significant but roughly comparable to ASML's technology from around 2001 -- about 25 years behind current EUV -- and semiconductor manufacturing capability is fundamentally 'learning by doing,' meaning China cannot simply leapfrog decades of process learning just by acquiring the hardware.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: China's lithography gap remains large and structurally slow to close, tempering fears that this development immediately threatens Western semiconductor equipment leadership.
insights.quote: let's just say a DUV machine was a jet turbine and now like an EUV machine is like a warp drive.

insights.claim: The stock-market selloff in semicap equipment names triggered by the China DUV news was likely an overreaction given the roughly 25-year technology gap, but the guest cautions the news shouldn't be dismissed either, noting the market has repeatedly cycled between panicking about and forgetting China semiconductor developments and it could take years for any real impact to show up in ASML's order book.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Semicap equipment stocks may see repeated bouts of China-related volatility disconnected from near-term earnings impact, creating potential mispricing opportunities on both sides.

insights.claim: US-China AI and semiconductor decoupling is now self-reinforcing on both sides and, in the guest's view, effectively irreversible at this point regardless of near-term technology gaps.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Investors should treat US-China tech decoupling as a durable, multi-decade structural trend rather than a negotiable near-term policy dispute when positioning in semiconductor and AI supply chains.
insights.quote: for for better or worse like we are decoupling and um just that is a process that has been set in motion and at this point it almost feels like it's kind of self-reinforcing on each side

themes.theme: SpaceX as an Underappreciated AI Infrastructure Play

insights.claim: SpaceX is reportedly monetizing its compute buildout at roughly $50 billion per gigawatt currently, with consensus estimates for next year rising to about $73 billion per gigawatt -- figures the guest says the public market has not digested because SpaceX still isn't broadly understood as a compute/AI-infrastructure company.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: If these monetization figures hold, SpaceX's compute business alone could become a material, underappreciated revenue driver not reflected in how the stock is currently valued or discussed.
insights.quote: they're monetizing at something like 50 billion a gig. And consensus estimates for next year are 73 billion.

insights.claim: To date, only the major hyperscalers plus CoreWeave, Crusoe, and SpaceX have brought on more than 500 megawatts of power capacity in a single year, and SpaceX has done so at both the fastest pace and the lowest cost among them.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: SpaceX's demonstrated ability to stand up large-scale power/compute capacity faster and cheaper than nearly anyone else is an operational edge that should factor into any bull or bear case on the stock.

insights.claim: A prominent New York hedge fund reportedly holds a short position on SpaceX premised on spot GPU compute prices falling roughly 90%, but the guest believes very little of SpaceX's potential compute buildout is priced into consensus estimates and cites Elon Musk's history of eventually delivering on ambitious infrastructure targets, even late.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: A well-known short thesis on SpaceX rests on an assumption (a 90% spot price collapse) that directly contradicts the accelerating spot-price data described elsewhere in this conversation, making it a key thesis to monitor for a squeeze or vindication.
insights.quote: one of Elon's phrases is we specialize in making the impossible late

insights.claim: When SpaceX brought a large amount of compute capacity into the market via Blackwell/B200 cluster sales and rentals, the market absorbed it entirely without any price disruption, which the guest cites as evidence of how compute-starved the overall market currently is.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: The market's ability to absorb a sudden large compute supply increase without a price drop is a strong real-world signal of underlying demand tightness, supporting the broader bull case on AI infrastructure pricing.
insights.quote: It was like the market just utterly absorbed it, you know, like just the freight train didn't slow down at all.

themes.theme: AI Labor Substitution, Token Spend, and the Regulatory Threat

insights.claim: Companies with heavy AI adoption report AI/token spend running at roughly 20-25% of total compensation spend, with one company cited at 30% (among the highest reported) and anecdotal reports as high as 50% at some firms -- figures the guest uses to size a potentially multi-trillion-dollar shift, since global knowledge-work spend is roughly $25 trillion and even a 20% substitution rate implies about $5 trillion in addressable spend.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Token spend as a percentage of total compensation is becoming a trackable KPI for how far AI substitution has progressed inside a company, and the 20-30% range at leading adopters implies a very large addressable market still in early innings.

insights.claim: Public data referenced from Cognition, Ramp, and Stripe (the 'Cognition index') shows companies that spend the most on AI are growing meaningfully faster than peers, though the guest acknowledges the data doesn't control for industry mix, a fair criticism from skeptics.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: This correlation, while not fully controlled, is one of the few concrete cross-company data sets linking AI spend directly to revenue growth, and is worth tracking as it matures.

insights.claim: Founder-controlled companies -- who, adjusted for COVID-era overhiring, are not conducting large-scale layoffs despite being among the fastest AI adopters -- suggest that the leading indicator among the most AI-savvy operators is confidence in future growth opportunity for their workforce, favoring the 'faster economic growth' bull case over the 'labor substitution' bear case for AI's macro impact.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Watching layoff/hiring trends specifically at founder-controlled, AI-forward companies is a useful proxy for whether AI's macro impact skews toward growth-accretive or purely labor-displacing.

insights.claim: The guest estimates only about 500,000 people worldwide currently use agentic AI even as the industry describes itself as in an 'acute compute shortage' -- against a global population of 7-8 billion, implying enormous unaddressed demand runway if usage moves from 500,000 toward even 1% (roughly 100 million) or several hundred million users.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: This framing suggests current AI compute shortages reflect an extremely early stage of adoption, implying that even modest gains in penetration could sustain compute demand growth for years, independent of any single model or company's trajectory.
insights.quote: 500,000 people in the world 250,000 maybe are using agentic AI and we're in an acute compute shortage

insights.claim: The guest identifies regulation as the biggest risk to the AI buildout, citing New York's data center moratorium as the leading edge of a broader political backlash, and argues the AI industry has done a poor job of public relations, letting a narrative take hold (that data centers raise electricity prices, drain water, and destroy jobs) that is largely false: behind-the-meter deals typically lower local electricity prices and data center construction adds sustained blue-collar trade jobs.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: Regulatory backlash driven by a false public narrative is the risk factor the guest views as most likely to actually derail the AI buildout, more than compute economics or credit -- worth tracking state and local data center policy closely.
insights.quote: I think regulatory has to be the biggest risk.

insights.claim: A widely cited claim about massive data-center water consumption traces back to an author's book that overstated data-center water usage by roughly four orders of magnitude (about 10,000x), an error the author has since admitted and that has been thoroughly debunked -- yet the false figure continues to circulate, a dynamic the guest compares to the persistent myth that spinach is unusually high in iron (also traced to a misplaced decimal point in an old academic source).
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: This illustrates how a single debunked but widely repeated statistic can drive real policy outcomes (like data center moratoriums), underscoring why the guest sees industry PR/communications as a genuine investment risk factor, not just a soft issue.
insights.quote: an author made a mistake in a book and overestimated the amount of water usage in data centers by 10,000 necks.

themes.theme: Frontier of Infrastructure Innovation: SRAM Chips and Continual Learning

insights.claim: Disaggregating AI inference into three separately optimized hardware stages -- prefill (which doesn't need HBM DRAM), attention (which needs high-bandwidth HBM DRAM), and the feed-forward network (best served by SRAM-based accelerators built on older, non-cutting-edge chip nodes) -- is, in the guest's view, one of the biggest underappreciated levers for improving AI infrastructure ROI, since no single chip design can optimize the ratio of compute to HBM to SRAM for constantly changing workloads.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: SRAM-based accelerator companies targeting the feed-forward-network portion of inference represent an underappreciated investment category poised to improve overall AI infrastructure returns even without new leading-edge GPUs.
insights.quote: You just can't beat SRAAM in particular for that feed forward network

insights.claim: The guest flags progress toward solving 'continual learning' and 'sample-efficient learning' (training capable models on far fewer tokens -- potentially 10 trillion versus the roughly 300 trillion tokens used by current frontier models) as the one scientific development that could meaningfully disrupt AI infrastructure training demand; Safe Superintelligence (SSI) has said it plans to release a model addressing this in August, though the guest still doesn't think it would be net negative for infrastructure demand given how small training already is as a share of total compute relative to inference.
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: A breakthrough in sample-efficient/continual learning is the single technical development most likely to reduce AI training compute demand, and is worth monitoring via SSI's upcoming model release and any similar announcements from other labs.

insights.claim: Asked to name a 'dark horse' company or person that could become as systemically important as Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, Amazon, or Nvidia, the guest named a Fireworks AI executive referred to as 'Lynn,' calling her 'an absolute killer,' as well as Cognition (led by a person referred to as 'Scott Woo').
insights.speaker: Gavin (guest, AI-focused fund investor)
insights.so_what: These are the specific private companies/people the guest personally flags as most likely to surprise the market with outsized future importance in the AI stack.
insights.quote: I do think um Lynn at Fireworks, she is like a just an absolute killer.
